problem: ☂️ and 🌂 are both umbrellas and both accepted, so two of the three options are right and a guess succeeds 2 times in 3.

problem: "Fire is safe to touch." is spoken as a statement to young children; the unsafe idea is what they hear and may keep.
evidence: Rule 11 (kind, true and safe); children with language difficulties often remember the proposition and lose its truth value. The answer stays No.

problem: "the green man" is a UK/Irish term for the walk signal; learners elsewhere may not know it.

fix.audio_text: We wait for the green light to cross.

evidence: Rule 12 (local and fair); "green light" is understood everywhere. Same fix as EN-RD-T03-Q05.

problem: The spoken sentence has 10 words with a clause at level 1.

fix.audio_text: When lost, we tell a grown-up we trust.

evidence: Rule 1 (at most 8 words per sentence at levels 0-2); Gathercole & Alloway (2008): long spoken sentences overload working memory.

problem: The hint "Once a year? Really?" is sarcastic; literal learners may not read the tone.

fix.hint: How many times a day do you brush your teeth?

evidence: Rule 2 (literal language): sarcasm is hard for autistic learners and learners with DLD (Vulchanova et al. 2015).

problem: The word to hear is "tap", which is printed in the instruction ("Tap the first letter") and on the action strip, so a reader sees its first letter.

problem: The hint "Say buh-ag." adds an "uh" to the first sound.

fix.hint: Say it slowly: b-ag. Keep the b short.

evidence: Adding "uh" to a stop sound (buh, duh) teaches a sound that is not in the word and makes blending harder; phonics teaching uses pure sounds (DfES Letters and Sounds 2007; Ehri 2005).

evidence: Picture and word must name the same thing (rule 5); the hint "Two are ways to move" still fits.

problem: "I wash my hair before dinner" is also a sensible sentence, so "hair" is defensible.
evidence: One defensible answer per item; the hint ("What touches your food?") assumes hands. Same fix as EN-RD-T04-Q01.

problem: Rubbish also goes "in the bag" (a bin bag), so "bag" is defensible; the hint says the bin "lives" in the kitchen.

fix.hint: It has a lid. It is in the kitchen.

evidence: One defensible answer per item; rule 2 (literal: bins do not live). Same fix as EN-RD-T04-Q02.

problem: Both "purse" and "pocket" are accepted, so two of three options are right, and the hint "It zips up" fits only purse.
evidence: One defensible answer per item (rule 10). Same fix as EN-RD-T04-Q07.

problem: A caterpillar that becomes a butterfly makes a chrysalis; cocoons are made by moths.

fix.audio_text: First the caterpillar eats. Then it makes a chrysalis. Then it becomes a butterfly.

evidence: Rule 11 (true content); life cycles are in primary science (NCCA, National Curriculum England), so the English bank should not teach the wrong word.

problem: 🥤 is a cup with a straw, not a bottle.

problem: "Tap all the healthy snacks" sorts foods into healthy and unhealthy, and the hint "grow from the ground" is wrong for apples.

fix.hint: Two of them are fruit or vegetables.

evidence: Rubric wellbeing wording: foods are "everyday" or "sometimes", never good/bad (HSE/safefood guidance).

problem: "push in the queue" is a UK idiom (US "cut in line"), and taken literally "push" describes a different act.
evidence: Rule 2 (literal language) and rule 12 (local and fair). The correct answers are unchanged.

fix.audio_text: Sara has two sweets. Her friend wants one. Can she share?

evidence: Rule 9: no negation at levels 0-2 (Nordmeyer & Frank 2014); rule 1: at most 8 words per sentence.

problem: The prompt "What should I do now?" and options "wash my hands" ask the learner to answer as the speaker; "I/my" here means someone else.

evidence: Shifting pronouns are hard for autistic learners and learners with DLD (Lee, Hobson & Chiat 1994); "you" matches the other items.
